newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright to discuss NATO, arms on Russian visit.
newsitem.headline: Albright to discuss NATO, arms on Russian visit.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrives in Russia on Saturday for talks with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, her tough but respected sparring partner in months of wrangling over NATO expansion.

Albright, who lands in St Petersburg around 6 p.m. (1400 GMT), is expected to brief Primakov on this week's NATO summit in Madrid, where the formal decision to expand eastward was taken. She will also raise outstanding arms control issues.

Diplomats say she will be seeking to build on improving relations with Moscow -- despite fierce arguments over NATO -- but officials have not disclosed the precise agenda during her 19-hour stay in Russia's former tsarist capital.

Primakov, who has built up a considerable personal rapport with the equally feisty Albright despite their fierce duelling since she took office six months ago, embodies Moscow's bitter opposition to the enlargement of its old Cold War adversary.
On Tuesday, he called the invitations issued to former Soviet satellites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic "the biggest mistake in Europe since the end of World War Two".

Albright's visit, sandwiched between talks in prospective NATO members Slovenia and Lithuania, is part of a series of whistle-stop European tours by U.S. leaders, including President Bill Clinton, following the Madrid summit.

It also opens a round of diplomatic house calls on Russia by Western foreign ministers. British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook will be in Moscow on Monday and Tuesday. Germany's Klaus Kinkel will discuss NATO with Primakov on Tuesday in the capital.
All are expected to stress the West's willingness to improve ties with Russia and to develop its cooperation with NATO which was enshrined in the NATO-Russia Founding Act signed in May.

That treaty, thrashed out over months of intense diplomatic activity, sought to answer some of Moscow's fears and objections raised by NATO expansion by giving it a say in the alliance's affairs and offering assurances on deployment of NATO forces.
Russian officials, too, have pledged to enhance cooperation and not to dwell on their differences.
U.S. officials say Albright and Primakov will discuss international negotiations on updating a 1990 treaty limiting conventional arms in Europe and where they are deployed.
They are also expected to discuss the START 2 nuclear arms pact between Moscow and Washington cutting strategic warheads.

President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, said on Saturday that parliamentary ratification of START 2 would be one of Russia's toughest foreign policy issues in the second half of the year, along with debate in the opposition-dominated parliament on the NATO-Russia Founding Act.

"On START 2, the State Duma (lower house) deputies are quite right, in my view, to demand additional expert evaluations, in particular, from the defence and foreign ministries, and a deeper analysis of the consequences of ratifying the agreement," he told Interfax news agency, adding that Yeltsin agreed.
It was not clear whether Russian objections to a NATO swoop on suspected war criminals in Bosnia, which Russia denounced on Friday as "cowboy raids", would be raised in St Petersburg.
Primakov and Albright will talk over dinner at a restaurant on Saturday evening and tour the Hermitage art gallery in the tsars' Winter Palace, focus of the 1917 Bolshevik coup d'etat.
On Sunday morning, the Secretary of State will hold further talks with Primakov over coffee at her hotel.
